text: Five quick ones, on the vocabulary. A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. A discrete one has a mass function: each value's probability. A continuous one has a density, where probability is area, so a single point has probability zero, and the height can pass one, as a narrow normal's does. The distributions to know: Bernoulli and binomial for yes-or-no outcomes and their counts. Normal for symmetric data, and for means. Poisson for rare-event counts, where the mean equals the variance. Uniform for equal chances, exponential for waiting times. Their supports and moments say which likelihood fits. Sampling: simple random gives every unit the same chance. Stratified samples within groups, so each one shows up, like a rare class in every test set. Cluster sampling takes whole groups, to cut cost. Reservoir sampling handles a stream. Covariance says whether two variables move together, but its size depends on their units. Correlation divides by both standard deviations, landing between minus one and one, and it only sees straight lines: y equals x squared, on a symmetric range, has a correlation of zero. And correlation isn't causation: a confounder can drive both, as hot weather drives ice cream sales and drownings. A model can predict from a correlation. Deciding what to change needs a randomized experiment, or a causal method that rules confounders out. Minimizing log loss is maximum likelihood, and a deep network does it with millions of weights. Next: deep learning.
